goals: Explain the central idea of the poem stanza by stanza in your own words
Explain the movement of the trees from house to forest as a symbol of freedom
Interpret the speaker's silence and the poem's two readings
Answer extract-based and 40–50 word questions on the poem

slides.body_md:
*First Flight*, poetry · Class 10 CBSE English.

**Read the poem itself in your textbook, *First Flight* (NCERT), aloud, twice.** This lesson is SOYL's explanation; it does not reproduce the poem.

slides.narration: Welcome. Today's poem is The Trees by Adrienne Rich. It describes something impossible: trees that have been kept inside a house break out in the night and return to the forest. Please read it in First Flight now, aloud, twice. We will not repeat its lines here. Instead we will follow the escape, the speaker, the symbols and the devices.

slides.heading: How to read this poem
bullets: Read it aloud twice from *First Flight*; follow the pictures, not a rhyme.
Ask: where are the trees? what do they do through the night? what does the speaker do?
Then ask: what might the trees, the house and the forest stand for?
In answers, explain in your own words; never copy lines.
slides.narration: This poem has no regular rhyme, so read it for its pictures. Read it aloud twice. Ask where the trees are, what they do through the night and what the speaker does. Then ask the big question: what might the trees, the house and the forest stand for? In the exam, explain in your own words. Copying lines earns no marks.

slides.narration: Adrienne Rich was an American poet and essayist who lived from nineteen twenty-nine to two thousand and twelve. She was one of the leading feminist voices in American poetry, and she won the National Book Award in nineteen seventy-four for Diving into the Wreck. Knowing this helps us understand one reading of this poem.

slides.heading: The poem at a glance

rows: free verse in four stanzas; no regular rhyme or metre
a woman indoors, writing letters (first person)
trees kept inside a house break out and return to the forest
an empty forest → a night of struggle → a quiet speaker → a sudden break-out
the house (confinement), the forest (freedom), the trees (the confined)
calm and mysterious, becoming urgent and liberating

visual.alt: Table of the poem at a glance: free verse in four stanzas, a woman speaker writing letters indoors, trees breaking out of a house to return to the forest, a movement from an empty forest to a sudden break-out, the house, forest and trees as symbols, and a tone that moves from calm to urgent.

slides.narration: Here is the poem at a glance. It is free verse in four stanzas. The speaker is a woman sitting indoors, writing letters. The event: trees kept inside a house break out and return to the forest. The house, the forest and the trees are symbols. The tone begins calm and mysterious and becomes urgent and liberating.

slides.heading: Stanza 1: an empty forest
slides.body_md: In SOYL's words: the poem opens with news that the trees kept indoors are leaving for the forest. The forest has stood bare for days and nights: birds had nowhere to perch, insects nowhere to shelter, and the sun no shade to rest in. By dawn it will be filled again.
slides.narration: The poem opens with strange news. The trees that have been kept indoors are leaving for the forest. Then the poet looks at the forest. It has stood bare for a long time. Birds had nowhere to perch, insects nowhere to shelter, and the sun no shade to rest in. A forest without trees is hardly a forest. By dawn, it will be filled again.

slides.heading: Stanza 2: a night of struggle
slides.body_md: In SOYL's words: all night the roots labour to pull free of cracks in the veranda boards. Leaves press towards the windows, twigs grow rigid with effort, and the big branches, cramped for years under the roof, drag forward like dazed patients just released from hospital.
slides.narration: Now the struggle. All night the roots labour to pull free of cracks in the veranda boards. Leaves press towards the windows. Twigs grow rigid with effort. And the big branches, cramped for years under the roof, drag themselves forward like dazed patients just released from hospital. Freedom here is slow, stiff and hard-won.

slides.heading: Check: the simile
slides.narration: Your turn. The poet compares the branches to something. Which of these is the simile? Choose the best answer.

slides.heading: Stanza 3: the quiet speaker
slides.body_md: In SOYL's words: the speaker sits inside with the veranda doors open, writing letters in which she barely refers to the departure. The night is cool and clear, the full moon shines, and the scent of leaves drifts in, compared to a voice calling. Her mind is full of murmurs that will be quiet by tomorrow.
slides.narration: Meanwhile the speaker sits indoors with the veranda doors open. She is writing letters, and she barely refers to the trees leaving. The night is cool and clear, and a full moon shines. The scent of leaves drifts into the rooms, and the poet compares it to a voice calling. Her mind is full of murmurs. Why does she say so little?

slides.heading: Stanza 4: the break-out
slides.body_md: In SOYL's words: the last stanza tells us to listen. Window panes are shattering. The trees lurch out into the night, and the winds hurry to greet them. The moon itself seems to shatter like a looking-glass, and its fragments glitter at the top of the tallest tree.
slides.narration: The last stanza begins with a command: listen. Window panes are shattering. The trees lurch out into the night, and the winds hurry forward to greet them, as if welcoming them home. Then the moon itself seems to shatter like a looking-glass, and its fragments glitter at the top of the tallest tree. The trees are free.

slides.narration: Here is the whole poem as a flow. The forest stands empty. Roots and branches struggle all night. The speaker writes and says little. Panes shatter and the trees lurch out. The winds welcome them and the moon shatters. Notice the shape: a slow, quiet build-up and then a sudden, dramatic release.

slides.heading: Surface and depth
columns:
**On the surface**

- a house with a veranda
- potted trees
- woodland
- breaking glass

**Underneath**

- confinement
- women, or nature, kept for decoration
- freedom and growth
- an old order broken

visual.alt: Table of surface and deeper meanings: the house stands for confinement, the trees for women or nature kept for decoration, the forest for freedom and belonging, and the shattered panes and moon for an old order broken for ever.

slides.narration: Every element has a surface and a depth. The house is a home, but also confinement. The potted trees can stand for women kept within the home, or for nature kept as decoration. The forest is woodland, but also freedom and growth. And the shattering glass is the breaking of an old order, for ever.

slides.heading: Check: assertion and reason
slides.narration: Check yourself with an assertion and reason. Are both statements true? And does the second one explain why the comparison in the first one fits?

slides.heading: Themes and two readings
bullets: **Freedom:** every living thing longs to grow in its natural place.
**A feminist reading:** the trees as women confined to the home; the forest as the wider world.
**An environmental reading:** humans confine nature for decoration; nature reclaims its place.
**The cost of freedom:** escape is slow, painful and needs effort.
slides.narration: The themes follow. Every living thing longs to grow freely. Read one way, the trees are women confined to the home, and the forest is the wider world. Read another way, humans confine nature for decoration, and nature takes back its place. Either way, freedom is hard-won. In answers, give a reading and support it with images.

slides.narration: Now the devices. Personification runs all through the poem: roots labour, branches shuffle, winds greet. A simile likens the branches to dazed patients. Imagery appeals to sight and smell. The house, forest and trees are symbols. Lines run on in enjambment, and the whole poem is free verse. The examples on the right are our own sentences.

slides.heading: Worked point: the speaker's silence
slides.body_md: The poem never says why the speaker barely mentions the departure. We work it out from clues.
bullets: **Clue 1:** she leaves the veranda doors open.
**Clue 2:** she notices the night, the moon and the scent; she is not unaware.
**Meaning:** she quietly accepts, even supports, the trees' escape.
**Why it matters:** in the feminist reading, she may share their longing to be free.
slides.narration: Here is a worked point. Why does the speaker say so little? First clue: she leaves the doors open. Second clue: she notices the night, the moon and the scent, so she is not unaware. So she quietly accepts, even supports, the escape. In the feminist reading, she may share the trees' longing to be free.

slides.heading: Tone
slides.body_md: Calm and mysterious at first, quiet and dreamlike in the middle, then urgent and liberating at the end. The speaker never sounds alarmed by the departure.
slides.narration: Listen to the tone. The opening is calm and mysterious, stating something impossible as plain news. The middle is quiet and dreamlike: a cool night, moonlight and scents. The ending is urgent, full of breaking glass and rushing wind, and it feels liberating. Notice that the speaker never sounds alarmed. That tells us something about her.

slides.heading: Worked example: a 40–50 word answer
slides.body_md: *Question:* Why is the forest described as empty?
bullets: **Point:** its trees have been taken away and kept indoors.
**Image (own words):** birds, insects and the sun have nothing to use.
**Link:** the trees' return will restore the forest's life.

**Model (46 words):** *The forest has lost its trees, which humans carried off to decorate a house. Birds therefore find no branches, insects find no cover and the sun finds no shade. The forest cannot be itself until the trees come home, so their escape restores its life.*

slides.heading: Summary
bullets: Trees kept indoors set off for a forest that has stood empty without them.
All night they struggle; branches drag forward like dazed patients.
The speaker writes letters, barely mentioning it, with the doors open.
Panes shatter, the trees lurch out, the winds greet them, the moon seems to shatter.
Message: confined beings long for freedom. Read the poem in *First Flight*.

slides.narration: Let us sum up. Trees kept indoors set off for an empty forest. All night they struggle, and their branches drag forward like dazed patients. The speaker writes letters and barely mentions it, leaving the doors open. Then panes shatter, the trees lurch out and the moon seems to shatter. The message: confined beings long for freedom.

slides.heading: Exam tips
bullets: Never write out the poem's lines; describe each stanza in your own words.
Explain at least one symbolic reading: women, or nature.
Use the speaker's silence and the open doors as evidence.
40–50 word answers: point + image in own words + link to freedom.
Common slips: saying the speaker stops the trees; that the escape is easy; that the poem rhymes.
slides.narration: Exam tips. Never write out the lines; describe each stanza in your own words. Explain at least one symbolic reading. Use the speaker's silence and the open doors as evidence. Keep three mark answers to point, image and link. And avoid the slips: the speaker does not stop the trees, the escape is not easy, and the poem does not rhyme.

sections.heading: 1. The poet and the poem
sections.body_md:
**Read the poem itself in your textbook, *First Flight* (NCERT), aloud, twice.** This lesson is SOYL's explanation; it does not reproduce the poem.

**Adrienne Rich** (1929–2012) was an American poet and essayist, a leading feminist voice; she won the National Book Award in 1974 for *Diving into the Wreck*. *The Trees* describes an impossible event, trees breaking out of a house, and makes it a powerful image of freedom.

sections.heading: 2. What happens (SOYL summary)
sections.body_md:
**Stanza 1:** the trees kept indoors set off for the forest, which has stood bare: no perches for birds, no shelter for insects, no shade for the sun. By dawn it will be filled.

**Stanza 2:** through the night the roots labour to pull free of the veranda boards; leaves press towards the windows; twigs grow rigid with effort; cramped branches drag forward like dazed patients leaving hospital.

**Stanza 3:** the speaker sits inside with the doors open, writing letters that barely refer to the departure; a cool, clear night, a full moon, the scent of leaves drifting in like a calling voice; her mind full of murmurs.

**Stanza 4:** a command to listen; panes shattering; the trees lurch into the night; the winds hurry to greet them; the moon seems to shatter, its fragments glittering at the top of the tallest tree.

sections.heading: 3. Themes and message
sections.body_md:
- **Freedom:** every living thing longs to grow in its natural place.
- **The feminist reading:** the trees as women confined to the home by social expectations; the forest as the wider world; the speaker's silence as quiet sympathy.
- **The environmental reading:** humans uproot nature for decoration; the forest is lifeless without its trees; nature reclaims its place.
- **The cost of freedom:** escape is slow and painful, but once made it is final.

sections.heading: 4. Symbolism, devices and form
sections.body_md:
**Symbols:** the house (confinement), the forest (freedom and belonging), the trees (the confined), the shattered panes and moon (an old order broken).

**Devices:** personification (roots, branches, winds); simile (branches likened to dazed patients; the moon to a looking-glass); imagery of sight and smell; enjambment.

**Form:** free verse in four stanzas; long, run-on lines let one image tumble into the next.

key_terms.definition_md: Giving human actions or feelings to non-human things.
An object that stands for an idea (the forest for freedom).

**Extract-based (5 marks):** the board prints the poem's lines; SOYL practice uses commentary passages instead. Expect questions on the empty forest, the struggle, the simile, the speaker, the break-out and the symbols.

**Short answers (3 marks, 40–50 words):** point + image in your own words + link to the theme of freedom.

notes.exam_tips_md:
**Board weight:** reference-to-context extract (5) and short answers (3 marks, 40–50 words) on First Flight poems (CBSE 2026-27, Section C).

**How marks are awarded:** a correct point, support from the poem in your own words, and accurate expression within the word limit.

**Common mistakes**
1. Writing out the poem instead of explaining it.
2. Treating the poem as only about plants.
3. Saying the speaker tries to stop the trees.
4. Calling the escape easy or quick.
5. Mixing up the simile (dazed patients) with personification.

**Remember:** read the poem in your textbook, *First Flight*.

questions.passage_md: Adrienne Rich begins with a strange piece of news: the trees that have been kept indoors are leaving for the forest. Then she turns to the forest itself, which has stood bare for days and nights. Without its trees it cannot do what a forest should. Birds have no branch to perch on, insects have nowhere to shelter, and the sun has no shade to rest in. A forest without trees is hardly a forest at all. By dawn, the speaker says, that emptiness will be filled.

questions.passage_md: The second stanza shows the effort of escape. Through the night the roots labour to pull themselves free of cracks in the veranda boards. The leaves press towards the window panes, the small twigs grow rigid with effort, and the big branches, cramped for a long time under the roof, drag themselves forward. The poet compares them to patients just released from hospital, still dazed, making their way towards the clinic's exit. Freedom here is not easy or graceful. It is slow, stiff and hard-won.

questions.passage_md: Meanwhile the speaker sits indoors with the doors to the veranda open, busy writing letters. In them she barely refers to the most remarkable event of the night: the forest leaving her house. Is she unaware, or does she choose not to speak of it? Many readers sense that she knows exactly what is happening and keeps quiet, perhaps because she too longs to break free. The open doors matter. She is not trying to stop the trees. She lets them go.

questions.passage_md: The night around the house is cool and clear, and a full moon shines in a sky that is not yet closed in by branches. The scent of leaves and of the crusty growth on bark drifts into the rooms, and the poet compares the scent to a voice calling. questions.passage_md: The poem has four stanzas of free verse, with no regular rhyme or metre. Its lines often run on without punctuation, so that one image tumbles into the next, much as the trees push forward. answer.model_answer_md:
Night of the full moon

For years I stood in a pot on the veranda, admired by visitors, unable to stretch. Tonight I decided I would go. My roots ached as I worked them out of the cracks, one by one. My branches had forgotten how to move; I swayed like someone just out of hospital. Inside, the woman kept writing at her desk. She never looked up, but she had left the doors open, and I think she understood. When the panes gave way I stumbled out, and the wind came running to meet me. Now I stand among my kind. Birds are already settling on me. I am home.

The Editor
The City Times

Subject: Forests are not decorations

Sir,
I am writing to express concern about the uprooting of mature trees from nearby forests for decorative landscaping in new housing projects. In Adrienne Rich's poem The Trees, trees kept indoors struggle to return to a forest that has become lifeless without them. Our forests are suffering the same emptiness: fewer nesting birds, less shade, drier soil. Trees in pots and lobbies may look attractive, but they cannot support the life a forest does. I urge the authorities to ban such uprooting and to encourage native saplings instead. Let trees grow where they belong.

Yours faithfully,
Ananya Rao

checks.syllabus: topics t01–t04 only; no removed topics for 2026-27
checks.literature_rule: poem in copyright: no line or phrase reproduced (only the title and single words: veranda, disengage, exertion, boughs, lichen, crown); each stanza described in SOYL words, not paraphrased line by line; similes described, never quoted; device examples are SOYL sentences; extract items use SOYL commentary (passage_origin soyl-commentary); textbook pointer on the title slide, notes and every passage stem; forbidden-phrase guard (ch18 src/guard.mjs) run after the build
checks.accuracy: form (free verse, four stanzas) and stanza content checked; the speaker is a woman indoors writing letters, not one of the trees
checks.re_solve: author verifier pass: every item re-answered from its stem
checks.gate: npm test -w @soyl/content-templates and content lint (lintExemplar) run clean on this chapter
